name: Cleft sentences and preparatory it
subtitle: A cleft sentence puts the focus on one part of the message: It was Amira who called. What I need is a holiday. Preparatory it moves a long subject to the end: It's no use complaining.

flow.text: it points ahead to the real subject

concept.exampleHtml: It was Amira who called. — What I need is a holiday. — It's no use complaining.

qa.html: It is / was … that / who puts the focus on one word or phrase. Start with It is or It was, add the focus, then who (for people) or that (for everything else). Amira called me yesterday. → It was Amira who called me. — It was yesterday that she called. — It was my phone that broke. It was stays singular, even before a plural: It was my parents who paid.

What … is … puts the focus at the end of the sentence. I need a rest. → What I need is a rest. The same idea works with All I want is… and The thing that annoys me is…: All I want is a quiet evening. You can also focus on an action: She called the police. → What she did was (to) call the police.

To explain or to give a reason, use The reason (why) … is that or What happened was (that). The reason he left is that he was bored. — What happened was that the lights went out. After is or was you need a noun, a that-clause or to + verb.

Preparatory it stands in the subject position for a long clause that comes later. To complain is no use. → It's no use complaining. — That you can't come is a pity. → It's a pity that you can't come. The same happens after find, think, make, consider and appreciate: I find it hard to relax. — She made it clear that she was leaving. — I'd appreciate it if you could reply.

Typical mistakes: ✗ Is important to be on time. → ✓ It is important to be on time. (English needs a subject) · ✗ I find difficult to understand him. → ✓ I find it difficult to understand him. · ✗ It was Tom which called. → ✓ It was Tom who called. (who for people)

concept.noteHtml: Cleft sentences are for emphasis and contrast: It wasn't the price that bothered me, it was the service. In speech, stress the focus word. Not every it is preparatory. It's raining. It's ten o'clock. It's a long way. are ordinary uses (weather, time, distance). After what in What I need is… the what means the thing that: see Non-defining relative clauses. For the patterns after It's no use / worth / hard, see -ing or to and Gerunds.

tables.caption: Cleft sentences: moving the focus
head: Normal sentence
Cleft sentence
Focus
rows: {It was in Leeds that} we met.
{What she did was} (to) call the police.
He left because he was bored.
{The reason he left is that} he was bored.

tables.caption: Preparatory it: the patterns
head: Pattern
Example
rows: appreciate / like / hate + it + if / when
I'd appreciate {it} if you could reply.
{It} takes time to learn a language.

items: People: It was Amira who called.
Things: It was my phone that broke.
Time and place: It was in May that we met.
A person can also take that, but who is clearer.
✗ Is no use complaining → ✓ It's no use complaining
✗ I find hard to say no → ✓ I find it hard to say no
✗ What I need it is a rest → ✓ What I need is a rest
Weather and time: It's raining. It's late.

listen.text: It was Amira who suggested the new plan.
listen.note: Cleft sentence: the focus is Amira. Use who for a person.

listen.text: What I really need is a long holiday.
listen.note: What-clause + is: the focus comes after is.

listen.text: I find it hard to believe that he left.
listen.note: Preparatory it stands for the clause at the end.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose the words you hear. Listen for who, what and it.

items.text: It was Tom who broke the window.
What I need is a rest.
I find it difficult to concentrate.
It's a pity that you can't come.
The reason he left is that he was bored.

rounds.label: 1 · Put the focus on a word
rounds.instruction: You hear a normal sentence and a word in brackets. Say the sentence again as a cleft sentence with the focus on that word.

example.answer: It was Tom who paid the bill.

items.answer: It was Amira who broke the vase.
It was in Leeds that we met.
It was Kwame who called me this morning.

items.prompt: I lost my keys on the train. (my keys)
items.answer: It was my keys that I lost on the train.
It was Zofia who won the prize.
It was the delay that annoyed me.

rounds.label: 2 · Move the long subject: preparatory it
rounds.instruction: You hear a sentence with a long subject at the start. Say it again with It at the start and the long part at the end.

example.prompt: To drive in snow is dangerous.
example.answer: It's dangerous to drive in snow.

items.prompt: That you can't come is a pity.
items.answer: It's a pity that you can't come.

items.prompt: To explain it again is pointless.
items.answer: It's pointless to explain it again.

items.prompt: To get a seat on Friday is almost impossible.
items.answer: It's almost impossible to get a seat on Friday.

exercises.title: Which type of it?
exercises.hint: Is it a cleft sentence (focus), preparatory it (the real subject comes later) or an ordinary it (weather, time)?

exercises.title: who, that, what or is?
exercises.hint: Use who for people, that for things, times and places, what for the thing that.

exercises.title: Which word fills the gap?
exercises.hint: Preparatory it takes the place of the long clause. Choose the word that fits the pattern.

exercises.title: What goes together?
exercises.hint: Tap the start of the sentence, then the ending that fits.

exercises.title: Gap text: Why I left the committee
exercises.hint: Cleft sentences and preparatory it. Which small word fits each gap?
